newsitem.title: USA: Grand jury blasts N. California coliseum bond deal.
newsitem.headline: Grand jury blasts N. California coliseum bond deal.

text.p: A grand jury on Wednesday called on Oakland and Alameda County to restructure the terms of their $200 million football stadium project, warning the transaction could hurt their bond ratings.
The Alameda County grand jury, in an eight-page report issued in Oakland, urged local elected officials to change the way coliseum seats are sold.
The grand jury also sharply criticized the elected officials who worked on the transaction, which brought the National Football League Raiders back to Oakland and paid for coliseum improvements.

The grand jury's report followed this week's announcement that Oakland and Alameda County would have to pay out an estimated $8 million next fiscal year to cover debt payments on the $200 million coliseum bond deal.

The bonds were expected to be paid off through the sale of 10-year personal seat licenses (PSLs) and club seats, and with other revenues. But sales of seats and other stadium products have fallen $32 million short of projections and stadium construction costs have exceeded the budget by $30 million.
By failing to develop a "fall-back" for weak PSL sales, the grand jury said officials placed the "taxpayers at risk".
"It should have been apparent that the citizens of this community did not want public funds and additional taxes used for the Raiders' return (from Los Angeles)," the grand jury said.

The county panel alleged that some of the terms of the transaction were kept from the public, and it accused elected officials of accepting "staff projections of the salability of the PSL's without adequate inquiries."

The grand jury said the marketing of the PSLs was handled in "a less than professional manner," and warned that lagging PSL sales "could affect the future bond rating of the city and the county and the services now provided to all citizens."
The grand jury called for local officials to restructure the PSL plan to boost revenues and urged them to consider extending the life of the PSLs from the current 10 years to 15 years.
The panel also concluded that similar projects should, in future, be placed on the ballot for voter approval.
